title: Accuracy of Heart Rate Measurement with Wrist-Worn Wearable Devices in Various Skin Tones: a Systematic Review
authors: Koerber D, Khan S, Shamsheri T, Kirubarajan A, Mehta S
journal: Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
population: 10 studies, 469 participants stratifying HR or rhythm data by race or skin tone for consumer wrist-worn devices; Fitzpatrick score mean 3.5 (range 1-6) in six studies (n = 293)
findings: Four of ten studies reported a significant reduction in HR accuracy in darker-skinned participants; four reported no effect of skin tone; two showed mixed results.
The authors call the evidence preliminary and inconclusive, while noting some studies suggest wearables may be less accurate in participants with darker skin tones.
Higher-quality evidence is needed, with larger samples and more objective stratification by skin tone.
limitations: Only 10 small, heterogeneous studies with no pooled estimate and inconsistent skin-tone measurement; not running-specific. Year 2022 is the online date (print Dec 2023; Europe PMC lists 2023).
implications: Do not apply a skin-tone-specific correction factor; evidence is inconclusive.
Treat wrist-HR error as device and activity dependent, use an HR-quality flag with an sRPE fallback, and offer a chest-strap recommendation to every user who wants accurate HR load.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, J Racial Ethn Health Disparities, online 14 Nov 2022, print Dec 2023, first author Koerber. Abstract read. Downgraded evidence from A to B: a systematic review by design, but with 10 small studies, no synthesis and an inconclusive result. Added the conclusion that some studies suggest lower accuracy at darker skin tones; the researcher's implication about optional skin-tone collection is a design choice, not from the paper.
